openers.mesozoic-era: The Mesozoic opens on a wrecked world and a single giant landmass. Pangaea's land area had just peaked, and a megamonsoon of record strength swept across it, while even the poles lay free of ice. In the seas, shell-crushing and boring predators began an arms race that would reshape seafloor life for the whole era. On land, the plant-eater Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, and beaked rhynchosaurs joined a burst of new reptiles. Yet the Siberian Traps kept erupting, and the hottest stretch of the Phanerozoic held recovery back for millions of years.
openers.triassic-period: One supercontinent, one monsoon and no ice: that is the Triassic world. Pangaea reached its greatest land area after Siberia and the China cratons joined it, and its megamonsoon blew at full strength. Oxygen-poor seas and a searing Early Triassic climate, fed by repeated Siberian Traps eruptions, slowed life's return from the Great Dying. Still, new players appeared almost at once: rhynchosaurs, early neopterygian fishes, and coelacanths in their greatest burst of diversity. Microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow seas while the survivors regrouped.
openers.early-triassic-epoch: The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, and life paid for it. Oxygen-poor waters lingered, the Siberian Traps erupted again and again, and recovery from the largest mass extinction took millions of years. On land, Lystrosaurus made up as much as 90% of some faunas, while temnospondyl amphibians bounced back first. In the sea, microbial reefs spread, coelacanths diversified, and shell-crushing predators began the Mesozoic marine revolution. Across Europe, desert playas laid down the red Buntsandstein.

reviews.triassic-period: The Triassic was shaped by sheer size. Pangaea's land area peaked once Siberia and the China cratons joined, and that vast landmass drove a megamonsoon that brought rain to the once-dry Colorado Plateau. The greenhouse climate left even the poles without ice. Space rocks struck this world too, among them the impact that left North Dakota's buried Red Wing Creek structure, once wrongly tied to three other craters as a single event.
reviews.early-triassic-epoch: Every story in the Early Triassic runs back to the Siberian Traps. Their repeated pulses kept the climate the hottest of the Phanerozoic, starved the seas of oxygen and triggered fresh crises such as the Smithian–Spathian extinction. Recovery was slow and uneven: microbial reefs and Lystrosaurus herds filled the gaps first, and faunas looked much alike worldwide. Yet the same years produced the first frogs, ichthyosaurs, sauropterygians and dinosauromorph footprints. By the Latest Olenekian Cooling, as temperatures fell about 6 °C, the stage was ready for the Middle Triassic rebound.

tria-018.title: Pangaea's megamonsoon blows at full strength
tria-018.text: When nearly all the land on Earth sits in one block, the weather follows. The Pangean megamonsoon, a vast seasonal swing of wind and rain, reached its greatest strength in the Triassic. It peaked when Pangaea's land area was largest, after Siberia and the China cratons, ancient continental cores, had joined it. Its circulation may have reversed part of the global easterly winds, sending westerlies onto the west coast. Those shifting winds carried moisture to the previously dry Colorado Plateau. Meanwhile a greenhouse climate kept every continent free of ice, even at the poles.

tria-019.title: A buried crater scars North Dakota
tria-019.text: Some 2,000 m beneath McKenzie County, North Dakota, lies the scar of an ancient impact: the Red Wing Creek structure, about 9 km across. Thick Jurassic rocks fill the disturbed ground, which suggests a Triassic strike, and its age is estimated at 200 ± 25 million years. It was once grouped with Manicouagan, Saint Martin and Rochechouart as a single multiple impact. Those craters later proved to be millions of years apart.

tria-014.title: Shell-crushers launch the Mesozoic marine revolution
tria-014.text: On the Mesozoic seafloor, sitting still became dangerous. With the new era began the Mesozoic marine revolution, an arms race marked by more shell-crushing and boring predators and more animals bulldozing the seafloor. As predators grew steadily more capable, they stressed animals fixed in place. The balance shifted, because some prey adapted faster than others. Stalked crinoids, sea lilies anchored to the bottom, made easy targets for the shell-crushers from the Triassic on.

tria-009.title: Beaked rhynchosaurs appear in the aftermath
tria-009.text: Barely after the extinction, a new kind of plant-eater appeared: the rhynchosaurs, reptiles with beaks. They arose in the Induan, the first age of the Triassic, within a major diversification of reptiles. Early forms such as Noteosuchus come from the earliest Triassic of South Africa's Eastern Cape. Their peak came much later, in the Carnian, when they were abundant worldwide, and they died out early in the Norian.

tria-002.title: Stifling, acidic seas stall the ocean's recovery
tria-002.text: Poison gas drifted into sunlit shallows. Chemical fossils of green sulfur bacteria, microbes that need both light and hydrogen sulfide, show the gas reaching shallow water from the Late Permian into the Early Triassic. Oxygen-poor water lingered through the whole epoch, which may explain why sea life, especially on the seafloor, recovered so slowly. Persistently high carbon dioxide in air and sea also hampered shell builders. Seafloors flipping between oxygen-rich and oxygen-free states may explain the carbon-isotope swings of the time, shifts in the balance of heavy and light carbon.

tria-004.title: Desert playas lay down the red Buntsandstein
tria-004.text: From England to Poland, the ground of the Germanic Basin turned red. Arid playas, dry desert lake beds, laid down the Buntsandstein: red sandstones and conglomerates with little clay, holding small reptiles, plants and Chirotherium footprints. It is the first part of the three-part Germanic Trias, followed by the Muschelkalk and the Keuper. A major late Anisian rise in sea level ended it, flooding the basin with a tropical sea where the Muschelkalk began.

tria-005.title: Coelacanths and lungfishes enjoy their heyday
tria-005.text: Two famous 'living fossil' groups had their best days right after the worst disaster. Coelacanths, lobe-finned fishes, had their greatest burst of diversity in the Early Triassic, just after the Great Dying. Lungfishes reached their peak variety during the Triassic. Today only three lungfish genera survive.

tria-007.title: Pangaea bakes in the Phanerozoic's fiercest heat
tria-007.text:
At the equator, average temperatures may have reached 32–35 °C. The Early Triassic was the hottest stretch of the whole Phanerozoic, the age of abundant animal life. It came during and just after the Siberian Traps' huge release of greenhouse gases. Equatorial temperatures may have jumped 8–10 °C at the start of the Triassic. Pangaea's interior was mostly hot and arid, with widespread deserts, while even the poles were merely temperate.

The heat came in waves. A thermal maximum struck at the Permian–Triassic boundary. A brief Dienerian cooling followed, from 251 to 249 million years ago. Then came the Latest Smithian Thermal Maximum, about 249–248 million years ago. The toll on land may have been stark. Between about 30°N and 40°S, extreme heat may have left the land without tetrapods, four-limbed animals, from the Induan until the early Spathian.

tria-008.title: New-finned fishes arrive as ray-fins boom
tria-008.text: A predatory fish more than 1.2 m long, a saurichthyid, hunted Triassic waters as ray-finned fishes diversified remarkably, peaking in the Middle Triassic. Among them were the neopterygians, the 'new-finned' fishes. Their earliest unmistakable members, including early holosteans, appear near the start of the Triassic, though a Permian origin is suspected. Later in the period they became leading fishes of fresh and salt water, spreading through Norian seas as ceratitid ammonites declined.

tria-013.title: Lystrosaurus spreads to every corner of Pangaea
tria-013.text: In some of the earliest Triassic land faunas, nine animals in ten were the same beast. The pig-sized Lystrosaurus, a plant-eating dicynodont from the mammal-relative line, made up as much as 90% of some land vertebrate faunas. It was the most common land vertebrate and spread to every corner of Pangaea after the extinction. Trackways in South Africa's Karoo Basin show dicynodonts were abundant right after the crisis. Herding, tolerance of extreme and changeable climates, very fast growth and early sexual maturity probably explain its success. Some recent evidence questions its usual label as a disaster taxon, a species that booms in the wreckage of an extinction.

tria-015.title: Microbes build reefs in the extinction's wake
tria-015.text: With most reef animals gone, microbes took over the job. In the earliest Triassic, microbial reefs briefly spread across shallow, mostly low-latitude seas, in both oxygen-poor and oxygenated water. Mixed microbe–animal reefs, built partly by keratinous sponges, steadied many damaged communities. Microbial mats, thin carpets of microbes, left wrinkled surfaces at sea and on land. Their later disappearance signals burrowing animals returning as ecosystems recovered.

tria-022.title: The Siberian Traps erupt again and again
tria-022.text: The great eruptions that ended the Permian did not stop when the Triassic began. Swings in carbon isotopes and spikes of mercury suggest that massive Siberian Traps activity recurred several times in the Early Triassic. These pulses caused further extinctions and may have kept the climate hot. Later bursts are linked to the Smithian–Spathian, Olenekian–Anisian and Anisian crises. A release of methane, often blamed for such swings, cannot explain carbon-isotope shifts this large and this repeated.

tria-023.title: Life crawls back from the worst extinction ever
tria-023.text:
On land, full recovery took about 30 million years. That is how deep the wound of the largest mass extinction ran, and how harsh the Early Triassic climate was. Successive extinction waves and prolonged environmental stress held recovery back again and again. Early Triassic faunas were poor in species and much alike worldwide, the same few survivors turning up everywhere.

The sea healed faster, but not quickly. Seafloor communities stayed low in diversity until the end of the Early Triassic, about 4 million years after the extinction. On land, episodes of acidity stunted ecosystems well into the Triassic. Then, in the Anisian, marine recovery accelerated explosively. Crowded niches sharpened competition, and life began to diversify on every front.

tria-024.title: Temnospondyl amphibians bounce back first
tria-024.text: Big amphibians were the quickest to recover. Temnospondyls, a large group of extinct amphibians, peaked in diversity in the early Triassic, when most major stereospondyl subgroups, such as capitosaurs and trematosaurs, appeared. In the Induan they shrank, while tupilakosaurids thrived as disaster taxa. By the Olenekian they had regained their pre-extinction sizes. Then they declined through the Middle and Late Triassic, and only brachyopoids and trematosauroids survived beyond it.

tria-017.title: Moenkopi tidal flats redden the American Southwest
tria-017.text: Up to about 550 m of red rock records a coastline that came and went. Rivers, tidal flats and brief marine floods laid down the Moenkopi Formation's red sandstones and siltstones across the American Southwest. Its fossils point to a warm tropical climate, perhaps with monsoonal wet and dry seasons. Its Early Triassic bivalves, 27 species in 18 genera, cast doubt on the idea that bivalves recovered only in the Middle Triassic.

tria-021.title: Seas creep up from a Permian–Triassic low
tria-021.text: The Triassic began with the sea at its lowest. Sea level bottomed out at the Permian–Triassic boundary and stayed low through the period compared with other periods. Starting near today's level, it rose to about 10–20 m above present during the Early and Middle Triassic. The rise sped up in the Ladinian and peaked in the Carnian, at up to 50 m above today's level.

tria-025.title: Guiyang fossils capture an entire marine food web
tria-025.text: From grazers to top predators, a whole ocean community survives in one set of rocks. The Guiyang biota, from China's Daye Formation, is an exceptionally preserved late Induan assemblage dating to about 250.8 million years ago. It holds every trophic level, every rung of the food chain, from primary consumers to apex predators. So soon after the extinction, the sea already had a complete food web.

tria-027.title: Cynodonts and dicynodonts rise among the survivors
tria-027.text: Of all the therapsids, the mammal-relative group, only three lines made it through: dicynodonts, therocephalians and cynodonts. Cynodonts and dicynodonts soon dominated, and among dicynodonts only the stocky kannemeyeriiforms thrived. Cynognathians led the Early and Middle Triassic cynodonts, and Cynognathus was a top predator of Olenekian and Anisian Gondwana. Around 240 million years ago cynodonts diversified again, and plant-eating traversodontids peaked in the Late Triassic, mainly in Gondwana.

tria-029.title: Dinosaur cousins leave their first footprints
tria-029.text: The first hint of the dinosaur line is a set of footprints. Fossil footprints from the Olenekian are the first signs of dinosauromorphs, the group that holds dinosaurs and their closest relatives. Argentina's Chañares Formation preserves early dinosaur-like animals such as Lagosuchus and Lagerpeton. Their wider group, the avemetatarsalians, played only a minor part in Triassic ecosystems. Yet it eventually produced the first pterosaurs and dinosaurs.

tria-028.title: Dicroidium seed ferns take over Gondwana
tria-028.text: Across much of the southern supercontinent, the forests had fern-like leaves but bore seeds. Dicroidium, a seed fern, took hold around the Induan–Olenekian boundary and its trees came to dominate large parts of Gondwana through the Triassic. Its flora peaked in diversity in the Anisian. The end-Triassic extinction brought these ecosystems down, leaving only a relict in Antarctica.

tria-031.title: Triadobatrachus, the oldest known frog, appears
tria-031.text: About 250 million years ago lived Triadobatrachus massinoti, the earliest known frog. It belongs with the lissamphibians, the modern amphibians, which first appeared in the Triassic; frog forerunners were present by the Early Triassic. Stem relatives of salamanders and of caecilians, legless burrowing amphibians, also arose. Yet modern amphibians stayed uncommon until the Jurassic. They spread only as the older temnospondyls waned.

tria-032.title: Ichthyosaurs carry reptiles back to the sea
tria-032.text: Just two million years after the end-Permian extinction, reptiles were already heading back to sea. Ichthyosaurs, the 'fish lizards', evolved from land reptiles that returned to the water, much as the ancestors of whales and dolphins later did. They appeared around 250 million years ago, among the first marine reptiles. The oldest remains of their wider group, the ichthyopterygians, come from Olenekian rocks on Spitsbergen, and early forms lined northern Pangaea's coasts from Japan and China to Canada. Ichthyosaurs in the narrow sense arose about 245 million years ago, and by the Middle Triassic some were very large. The line endured until about 94 million years ago, in the Late Cretaceous.

tria-033.title: South China docks as Pangaea reaches its peak
tria-033.text: A single ocean, Panthalassa, covered almost 70% of Earth's surface. The rest was mostly one landmass. Pangaea reached its height about 250 million years ago, at the start of the Triassic. Around then South China collided with the Qinling complex and North China, joining the supercontinent and forming the Sichuan Basin.

tria-034.title: Mountain building strikes western North America
tria-034.text: Western North America crumpled twice in a row. Long after the Late Devonian Antler orogeny, the Sonoma orogeny, a new mountain-building episode, struck around the Permian–Triassic transition. It is linked to Sonomia, an island arc or small continental fragment, joining the continent's western edge. Not everyone agrees on the mechanism: some geologists dispute whether converging plates produced it.

tria-030.title: Colliding blocks piece together East Asia
tria-030.text: East Asia was built like a pileup. Between about 250 and 230 million years ago, the crustal blocks of Annamia, Sibumasu, Qiangtang and Lhasa collided with South China and each other, raising the Indosinian orogeny. This southern Asian landmass then hit North China, Tarim and other blocks about 240–220 million years ago, along the Central China orogen. That collision closed the Qinling ocean, and deep subduction destroyed part of the North China craton's root. Final closure of the Paleoasian Ocean, about 240–230 million years ago, joined Tarim and North China to Kazakhstan and Siberia. These additions gave Pangaea its greatest land area as climate changed sharply and the megamonsoon developed, though any link is still being studied.

tria-035.title: A second blow: the Smithian–Spathian extinction
tria-035.text: Life had barely started to recover when it was knocked down again. The Smithian–Spathian boundary event, the second extinction after the end-Permian one, struck during the Olenekian. The late Smithian crisis was a widespread ocean anoxic event, a spell when much of the sea lost its oxygen. Renewed Siberian Traps volcanism has been linked to it, and the Smithian closed with a thermal maximum around 249–248 million years ago. Grim episodes like this kept returning through the Early Triassic and delayed life's recovery. Idaho's Paris biota is the first diverse fossil assemblage known after it.

tria-036.title: Idaho's Paris biota marks a fresh start
tria-036.text: About 3 million years after the end-Permian extinction, a shallow sea off Pangaea's west coast teemed with life again. Idaho's Paris biota is an exceptionally diverse marine assemblage from the earliest Spathian, about 249 million years ago. Its animals lived in a near-equatorial sea, and beds with its ammonoids are dated to 248.853 ± 0.086 million years. It is the first diverse assemblage after the Smithian–Spathian extinction.

tria-037.title: Flipper-limbed sauropterygians take to the water
tria-037.text: Soon after the end-Permian extinction, another line of land reptiles traded legs for flippers. Sauropterygians, flipper-limbed marine reptiles, first appeared about 248–247 million years ago, in the Spathian, and were already notably diverse. With hupehsuchians and ichthyopterygians they were among the first marine reptiles, entering the scene in the Olenekian. They flourished through the Triassic. At the period's end, all but the plesiosaurs died out.

tria-039.title: A sharp cooling ends the Early Triassic heat
tria-039.text: The Early Triassic heat finally broke. During the Latest Olenekian Cooling, from 248 to 247 million years ago, temperatures fell by about 6 °C. The Middle Triassic stayed cooler, with temperatures falling through most of the Anisian. In those cooler Anisian oceans, reefs built by animals became common again.
